author: Marisa Roman
title: 12 Haunted Places In Texas You Can Visit Yourself - NewsBreak
text:
By Marisa Roman ,
3 hours ago
Texas holds more haunted places per square mile than a state this massive has any right to. Part of that comes down to its sheer age, but mostly, it’s about the staggering number of historic hotels, abandoned hospitals, and iron bridges that have stood for generations.
I’ve spent time chasing these local legends myself when I was on the road full-time, from spending an evening with the mystery of the Marfa Lights to sipping cocktails surrounded by the heavy history of The Driskill in Austin.
What follows isn’t a definitive ranking. Instead, it’s twelve haunted places with enough documented local lore that you can visit them yourself, plus one you’ll have to admire safely from the sidewalk.
1. Marfa Lights, Marfa Ron – stock.adobe.com The oldest unexplained thing in Texas, and the easiest to go see. Mysterious lights have been reported flickering above the Mitchell Flat east of Marfa since the 1880s, when a cowhand first assumed he was looking at Apache campfires. Theories since have covered everything from swamp gas to headlights on US 67.
There’s a state-built viewing area on US 90 about nine miles east of town, open around the clock and free. Go after full dark and give it an hour. You’ll see something or you won’t, and either way the sky out there is worth the drive.
2. Goatman’s Bridge (Old Alton Bridge), Denton Neff Conner – Flickr Officially, it’s the Old Alton Bridge, an iron truss bridge built in 1884 over Hickory Creek. The legend attached to it is grim, and worth labeling as legend: the story goes that a Black goat farmer named Oscar Washburn was lynched from the bridge by Klan members in the 1930s, and that a goat-headed figure has haunted it since. The lynching is repeated across local sources, but we could not find it in any primary record, so treat it as unverified local folklore rather than documented history.
The bridge is closed to cars and open to foot traffic, part of a public trail system south of Denton. It’s one of the most searched haunted sites in the state and gets busy on October weekends. Worth going on a weekday if you’d rather have it quiet.
3. Grand Galvez (Formerly Hotel Galvez), Galveston Victoria Ditkovsky – stock.adobe.com Built in 1911 on the Seawall to convince the country Galveston had recovered from the 1900 hurricane, and renamed Grand Galvez in 2021 after new ownership took over. Locals still call it the Galvez.
The haunted room is 501, attached to a woman remembered as Audra, who is said to have hanged herself in a turret in the 1950s after hearing her fiancé’s ship was lost. Guests report faucets and lights working on their own. Room 501 is booked so far in advance for October that the hotel’s own ghost tour guide has said you need to reserve it a year out. The hotel leans into it all and runs guided ghost tours year-round.
4. USS Lexington, Corpus Christi nevskyphoto – stock.adobe.com A World War II aircraft carrier turned museum, permanently moored in Corpus Christi Bay. The ship saw combat across the Pacific and lost crew members aboard, and the stories tend to involve a helpful sailor in dungarees who gives visitors directions in the engine room and then isn’t there anymore.
It’s a full museum with regular daytime hours, so this is the most family-workable stop on the list. The ship also runs overnight programs, which is a different experience entirely.
5. Menger Hotel, San Antonio Gerald Zaffuts – stock.adobe.com Open since 1859 and sitting directly beside the Alamo, which gives it a head start on atmosphere. The most repeated story belongs to Sallie White, a chambermaid killed by her husband in 1876, whose burial the hotel paid for. Teddy Roosevelt recruited Rough Riders in the bar.
Still a working hotel. You can walk into the bar and the lobby without staying the night.
6. Emily Morgan Hotel, San Antonio philipus – stock.adobe.com Also next to the Alamo, and it was a medical building before it was a hotel: offices, a morgue, and a crematorium in the basement. That history does most of the work here. Guests report elevators moving on their own and phones ringing at the front desk when no one is there.
7. Yorktown Memorial Hospital, Yorktown Nicholas Henderson – Flickr A Catholic hospital that operated from 1950 to 1988 in a small town southeast of San Antonio, with a reputation so strong that paranormal groups have investigated the building for years. It’s privately owned rather than a public site, so access depends entirely on what the owners are offering at the time. Check before you drive out. We’ve written in more detail about what happened inside this building .
8. The Driskill, Austin Fotoluminate LLC – stock.adobe.com Built by a cattle baron in 1886 and still the grandest lobby in downtown Austin. The stories cluster around a senator’s daughter who died in a bathtub fall, a bride in the same room decades later, and a painting of a young girl holding flowers that people swear tracks them across the room.
Working hotel, central location, easy to walk through.
9. Jefferson Hotel, Jefferson Nigar – stock.adobe.com Jefferson is a small East Texas town that was a major riverport before the railroad went elsewhere, and the whole place trades on its own history. The hotel dates to the 1850s as a cotton warehouse and has a guest book at the front desk where visitors have written down what happened in their rooms. That book is the real attraction.
10. Presidio La Bahía, Goliad mansfieldphoto.com – stock.adobe.com A Spanish fort from 1749, and the site of the Goliad Massacre in 1836, when several hundred Texian prisoners were executed by Mexican forces. The history alone earns its reputation. You can tour it during the day, and the site rents out a set of quarters overnight, which is an unusually direct way to test a ghost story.
11. Devil’s Backbone, Wimberley Melissa Pierce – Alltrails A limestone ridge along Ranch Road 32 in the Hill Country, and one of the prettiest drives in Texas in daylight. The stories are old and layered: Spanish monks, Confederate soldiers, a Comanche rider. The drive is public and free.
12. La Carafe, Houston Sean Davis – Flickr The oldest commercial building in Houston, put up around 1860, is now a small, candlelit wine bar on Congress Street, with bottles stacked to the ceiling. Staff talked for years about a former owner still tending the upstairs. It’s cash-preferred, tight, and not remotely a tourist trap, which is most of its charm.
One You Can Only Look At: The Baker Hotel, Mineral Wells Ross – stock.adobe.com Fourteen stories of 1929 Spanish Colonial Revival towering over a town of about 15,000, closed since 1972, and the single most photographed abandoned building in Texas. It’s under restoration, which has been going on since 2019.
One caution: Do not plan a visit inside. The reopening has been repeatedly delayed, and the most recent reporting puts it in 2028. As of May 2026, the roof, windows, doors, and asbestos work were finished. For now, it’s a building you look up at from the sidewalk, which is still worth the stop. Here’s more on the restoration .
If you want more Texas stories with a darker edge, there’s the urban legend that won’t die and the abandoned asylum outside San Antonio .
Which of these have you actually been to? Tell us what happened, and send this to whoever you’d drag along.
